overview.summary: Biotechnologists use living things, such as cells, bacteria and enzymes, to develop products and processes in areas like medicine, food, farming and the environment.
overview.problems: They help make medicines, vaccines, sustainable materials and better crops, and find new ways to clean up pollution.
overview.worksWith: Other scientists, technicians, doctors, engineers, regulators and company managers.
overview.workplaces: Laboratories in universities, hospitals, pharmaceutical and food companies, research institutes and start-ups.

timeline.title: Plan experiments
timeline.description: The biotechnologist reviews the day's tasks and safety steps.
timeline.why: Experiments need careful planning and safe procedures.

timeline.title: Laboratory work
timeline.description: The biotechnologist prepares samples, grows cells or bacteria in controlled conditions and runs tests.

timeline.title: Recording data
timeline.description: The biotechnologist writes careful notes of what was done and observed.
timeline.why: Records let others repeat and trust the work.

timeline.title: Analyzing results
timeline.description: The biotechnologist uses statistics and software to understand the data.
timeline.why: Data only helps when it is interpreted correctly.

timeline.title: Team meetings
timeline.description: The biotechnologist shares findings and plans next steps with colleagues.
timeline.why: Biotechnology projects need several kinds of specialist.

timeline.title: Repeating and checking
timeline.description: Many experiments fail or need to be repeated.
timeline.why: Science depends on results that can be repeated.

responsibilities: Designing and carrying out laboratory experiments
Following safety and ethical rules for working with living material
Developing and testing products or processes
Working with quality and regulation requirements
Keeping equipment and samples in good condition
challenges: Experiments often fail or give unclear results.
Research takes a long time and funding is limited.
Safety, ethics and regulation requirements are strict.
The work is detailed and repetitive.
Competition for research positions is strong and advanced degrees are often needed.
Long hours can be needed when experiments have to be monitored.
workEnvironment: Laboratories with equipment, protective clothing and strict safety rules, plus offices for analysis and writing. Hours are usually regular but experiments can require extra monitoring. Some roles are in manufacturing or quality control.
rewards: Contributing to medicines, food and environmental solutions
A mix of hands-on and analytical work
tradeoffs: Pay and opportunities that vary by country and sector

activity.title: Watch yeast make gas
steps: With an adult, put half a teaspoon of dried baker's yeast, a teaspoon of sugar and warm, not hot, water in a clean plastic bottle.
Stretch a balloon over the top.
Watch for 30 minutes and record any changes.
Repeat with no sugar and compare.
Write what you think the yeast did and why.
activity.outcome: You practise running a fair test and observing a living process.
activity.safety: Use only baker's yeast, sugar and warm tap water in plastic bottles, with adult supervision. Do not taste anything, do not try to grow bacteria or unknown organisms, wash your hands, and clean up when finished.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
